Existence of an infinite family of substrates satisfying all the
postulates of integrated information theory, exclusion included,
with arbitrarily large integrated information
Arnaud Mayeux
Abstract
Integrated information theory assigns to a physical system in a state a number Φ,
and declares a system to be a substrate of experience only if it prevails over all of its
subsystems in system integrated information. Upper bounds on Φ are known and grow
hyper-exponentially in the number of units. On the lower side there has been nothing.
We exhibit a family of substrates whose Φ is proved to grow, and which is proved to be a
complex. For every N ≥8 with 3 ∤N, let AN be the cycle of N binary units in which
each unit takes the exclusive-or of itself and its two clockwise neighbours. We prove two

that their “results are applicable even if a candidate system does not satisfy all the essential
properties”—exclusion being one of the five they list. Until a family is exhibited that prevails
over all of its subsystems and whose integrated information is proved to grow with size, the
interval between zero and the known ceiling is not known to be occupied at any point the
theory would call a subject.
There are two good reasons why this half of the question has proved the harder one.
The first is the mathematics itself, which is unusually resistant. Integrated information is
not an average or a smooth functional of a system’s parameters. It is defined through several
optimizations nested inside one another: over every way of carving a system into parts, taking

examples that circulate informally rather than in print, that highly expansive architectures
give large values of the bipartition-normalized measure used in earlier formulations of the
theory. Both are genuine sources of insight, and both leave open the question at issue here,
which is not whether large values occur but whether they occur on a substrate the theory
